object.medium: Relief carved into two granite boulders
object.description: Carved across two granite boulders at Mamallapuram on the Coromandel coast, this is the largest bas-relief in the world: 29 metres wide and 13 metres high, with more than a hundred figures of gods, people and animals. Tamils call it Arjunan Tapasu (அர்ச்சுனன் தபசு), Arjuna's Penance, after the gaunt figure standing on one leg beside the central cleft; the other reading is that he is Bhagiratha, whose austerities brought the river Ganges down from heaven to earth. The cleft between the boulders, which once carried real water from a tank above, stands for the river, and serpent-deities (nagas) rise in it. To its right walks a family of life-size elephants, among the most admired animal sculptures in India. The relief was cut in the mid-seventh century under the Pallava king Narasimhavarman I, called Mamalla, the great wrestler, from whom the town takes its name. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram.
facts: At about 29 by 13 metres it is the largest open-air rock relief in the world.
A cistern above the cleft once released water down the channel so that the Ganges actually flowed between the carved nagas.
The elephants are carved at life size; a sly cat 'doing penance' among mice beneath them is a famous joke in stone.
An unfinished copy of the same composition stands a few hundred metres away, abandoned by the Pallava carvers.
